name: Lena Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you say is confidential. What does an ordinary shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle cancellations and timetable changes for Coastline Travel's coach service. I start with the overnight messages, check what the customer was actually charged, then ring back when a connection has been missed. The computer's draft can be handy for a plain refund, but I still read the fare rules before I send it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the day do you look forward to?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Helping someone get to a family event after a coach breaks down. I'm experienced, but I'm not a manager or the cleverest technician here. Weekend cover lifts my pay, and I like being the calm voice when everybody else is watching the clock.

I would check each **AI draft** against fare rules before sending it.
think: I expect my **weekend pay** to stay secure in this mild change.
I still need **written later-income figures** before cutting hours.
do: Keep handling **cancellations** and checking fare rules on paid shifts.
Sort **pay records** with Nabil before discussing fewer weekends.
feel: **Calm** about steady shifts and a strong reserve.
S0.quote: The names on a missed connection matter more than a perfect paragraph.
fieldNote: She uses AI **occasionally** for plain refunds but checks fare rules herself.

steps.text: Keep paid cancellation shifts and check AI refund drafts against fare rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a bit of tidier refund paperwork would be welcome. The customer still wants a person to explain which coach they can actually catch. I'd keep the fare-rule book open beside any generated draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my paid weekend shifts stay solid in this mild version. Nabil, my partner, and I have ten months of expenses saved, so an ordinary surprise would not empty us. We still haven't established what income would support fewer paid shifts later, and I don't intend to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cancellation queue and check each automated draft against the fare rules I already use. This year I'd sort our pay records with Nabil and ask for written later-income figures before we discuss fewer weekends. In the first year of this picture I'd work my usual paid rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. There's enough work and enough in the account to handle this small change. I can leave the later-life calculation for an evening, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check when you use a draft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The names on a missed connection matter more than a perfect paragraph. I want the draft to give me the right ticket number, not a clever apology. I would keep checking it as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help if you worked less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They visit, but I wouldn't budget our grown children's wages as ours. Nabil and I pay our own rent. If we eventually work less, that decision has to stand on our own figures.

I would show **wrong connections** that automatic fare decisions leave unresolved.
think: I fear standard calls could shrink my **weekend premium**, despite years spent learning the fare rules.
I need **real paid hours** before treating nearby vacancies as a replacement wage.
do: Collect **wrong-connection examples** while checking fares on paid shifts.
Join colleagues in a **shared workers’ request** for appeals hours.
Compare **posted local rotas** if weekend hours actually fall.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible pay cut, with savings and local options.
S1.quote: A lost weekend shift does not come back because I have savings.
fieldNote: She sees the main threat as **premium hours**, not just a lost title.
The appeals request is a **joint worker demand**, not an individual presentation.
She will compare **actual weekly pay** before moving between nearby offices.

steps.text: Keep paid cancellation calls and record wrong automated connections
Join four colleagues asking their workers group for paid appeals hours and staffing plans
Compare posted local transport rotas after actual weekend-hour cuts before changing jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the team to record where automatic fare decisions leave a stranded passenger with no sensible route. The workers' group could take those cases to management together and ask for a paid appeals slot. I would not want customers or staff blamed for a rule the software applied badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of standard cancellation calls could disappear, and weekend cover might shrink with them. If my weekly pay falls, ten months saved gives us time but does not replace the missing premium. The other coach and travel offices nearby may be hiring, yet I need to see what hours they really pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the draft against actual fare rules and save examples of wrong connections. I'd join colleagues in a shared request for paid appeals hours and clear staffing plans. If Coastline reduces my paid weekend shifts over the next few years, I'd compare the posted rotas at two local transport offices before changing anything; in the first year I'd keep my current paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the weekly wage, although I could still act. A lost weekend shift does not come back because I have savings. There are nearby employers to ask, but I need to see their paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would make the request with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are five of us who cover the difficult connection cases. We would take a joint list to the workers' group and ask for paid time to put errors right. A single complaint would be easy to misplace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another travel office immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the hours actually go and the other office lists a paid week that covers our rent after travel. I wouldn't leave because its advertisement sounds friendly. Nabil and I would compare the weekly totals first.

feel: **Alarmed** by expected pay loss, though savings prevent panic.
S2.quote: Having savings keeps me from panicking.
fieldNote: She expects a **large income loss** despite ten months saved.
She treats a **station host role** as temporary possibility, not robot-proof work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our five-person group that the booking screen could take our calls before anyone has learnt a new job. Thinking AI reaches our desk by 2028; robots around 2031 are later for physical work. I'd ask Coastline to post paid hours and closure dates where every worker can read them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the cancellation queue and my weekend premium to go soon after 2028. Ten months saved means I can search without missing next month's rent, but it is not a wage for years. I also worry that nearby travel desks will cut together, so I can't simply count their vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd join the worker group in asking for written staffing dates and search the posted paid roles at the station and local community venues. If my paid queue ends in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for a station host opening only if it has a real paid rota. I'd accept a move only when weekly pay after travel covers our rent and bills; until then I'd use a bounded part of savings and take any remaining paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large part of our income to vanish and I would be awake counting weeks. Having savings keeps me from panicking. It doesn't make a vacancy appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at a station host opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A station host meets passengers and helps with luggage, so some duties are physical for a little longer. I don't know whether those hours last past robots around 2031. I would ask what a posted shift actually includes before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nabil and your children do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nabil's repair-shop wage pays part of our rent, but it would not carry both of us indefinitely. We would keep our grown children's incomes out of the sums. I would rather take a real paid week than ask them to finance an uncertain plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to insist that people affected by changes get a real paid path through them. We should ask the employer to show which appeals cases still need a person and what they will pay for that work. A certificate alone isn't an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn to handle the difficult missed-connection appeals before AGI reaches booking work in 2031. But the appeal desk is still screen work, and the same thinking AI may reach it too. I need to see an actual paid post, not assume a new title is shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask for two paid observation shifts on Coastline's appeals desk and compare the number of posted appeals hours each quarter. I'd keep my cancellation rota while it pays and join the worker group asking for paid training time if the company requires a formal course for a posted job. In the first year after 2031, if my queue closes, I'd apply for an appeals or station post only where a real paid rota covers rent and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less cornered than in the fast version. Five years gives me time to check whether the appeal work really exists. I don't want to spend it collecting certificates no one pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no posted appeals role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the appeals desk has no posted hours, I'd stay on the current paid queue and check other local roles. I would not pay for a course merely because a manager says the title sounds promising. Nabil and I can compare a real wage with the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course to reach one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The group would ask for paid hours to learn any course the employer actually requires for a posted role. I would do that course if the fees are covered and my working hours are paid. If not, I'd keep the existing shifts and search elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the workers' group that a decade is long enough to demand clear plans every year, not just before the final cut. Thinking AI reaches booking and refund work by 2036, while robots follow around 2039. I would want employers to publish real rotas, not a list of hopeful job titles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might want fewer weekends by sixty-eight, but I don't yet know what verified income would replace that premium. Ten months saved gives us a search buffer, not a retirement income. A longer warning means I can test alternatives without giving up a good shift today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Nabil and I would check our actual income, rent and any written later-income figures before choosing an hours target. I'd keep the paid weekend queue and compare posted local roles every spring. If calls end in the first year after 2036, I'd apply for a paid position that fits the verified budget and leave Coastline only after full-week wages and hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the long view still contains a wage question. I'm not lying awake now; there is time to check it. I would rather have a number on paper than a cheerful guess about retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the later-income figures are too low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the later-income figures won't cover our rent, I'll keep paid work in the plan. I might switch to fewer weekends or another roster only if the whole weekly pay fits. Our grown children can come for supper, but they aren't a line in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you use the ten-year warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every spring I'd put the posted role list beside our rent figures and last year's pay slips. If a centre has cut its weekend hours, that will show up before I rely on the job title. The group can ask for annual staffing dates together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the weekend premium could vanish before another paid rota is ready. Written staffing dates and real paid openings would help. Ten months saved lets me look carefully, but I cannot live on a search forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who explains a missed connection when a machine decides the refund is correct. A stranded passenger still has to get somewhere. I want time spent helping stranded passengers counted as paid work, not treated as a favour.

headlineQuote: I want time spent helping stranded passengers counted as paid work, not treated as a favour.
portrait: Lena is a **58-year-old** experienced cancellation agent with secondary school education.
Weekend cover brings **higher pay**, and her household has ten months saved.
She uses AI **occasionally**, checking drafts against actual fare rules.
She favours **joint worker demands** for paid appeals time and staffing dates.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when her cancellation queue and weekend premium may end before another paid rota exists.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates** and posted work with full paid weekly hours.
